articles.title: House GOP shelves Pete Hegseth impeachment articles
articles.summary: House Republicans on Tuesday shelved a measure spearheaded by outgoing Rep. Thomas Massie (R-Ky.) that would have led to a vote on impeaching Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth. In a dramatic and tight 211-204 vote, the House voted to refer the resolution to committee, a move that essentially ends efforts to impeach Hegseth over the Iran…
articles.body:
House Republicans on Tuesday shelved a measure spearheaded by outgoing Rep. Thomas Massie (R-Ky.) that would have led to a vote on impeaching Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth.

In a dramatic and tight 211-204 vote, the House voted to refer the resolution to committee, a move that essentially ends efforts to impeach Hegseth over the Iran war and other issues until the next Congress, when Democrats will hold large majorities in the House and Senate.

No Democrats opposed advancing the measure in Tuesday’s procedural vote, while Massie was the only Republican to vote with Democrats. Rep. Kevin Kiley (I-Calif.), who left the GOP this year and was defeated in last week’s elections, voted with Republicans.

Massie, a vocal critic of the U.S. war against Iran, had introduced eight articles of impeachment against Hegseth. He previously said that if a motion to kill the resolution referring it to committee failed and the House proceeded to the articles themselves, he would have requested a vote on each of the articles separately.

Massie has emerged as a vocal critic of Hegseth and President Trump, who both backed a primary challenger against him earlier this year. Massie lost his primary to former Navy SEAL Ed Gallrein; Hegseth traveled to Kentucky to support Gallrein, who was subsequently elected to Congress last week.

But the electoral defeat didn’t stop Massie from reintroducing the articles of impeachment against the Pentagon chief on the House floor Monday. Massie accused Hegseth of violating the Constitution and other laws during U.S. military operations in Yemen, Iran, the Caribbean, the Eastern Pacific and with the military operation that seized Venezuelan President Nicolás Maduro from his country at the beginning of the year.

Three of the articles are related to the Iran war, which Massie has said has been conducted without authorization from Congress. He also said Hegseth had defied Congress’s vote to end the conflict in the Middle East.

The fourth article asserts that Hegseth’s orders led to the dismantling of safeguards within the Pentagon “necessary to distinguish civilian objects from military objectives,” leading to the killing of civilians. Massie argued in the fifth article that the Defense secretary is the “executioner” who directed the ongoing deadly boat strikes on both sides of South America, where at least 244 alleged “narco-terrorists” have been killed.

The Kentucky Republican also argued Hegseth’s actions against Sen. Mark Kelly (D-Ariz.) — including starting a disciplinary procedure that could result in a reduction in military rank over his message to U.S. service members that they can refuse illegal orders — equated to retaliation against protected speech.

“We’re not indicting him for being bad at his job. In fact, he was very effective at killing schoolchildren in Iran; he was very effective at extrajudicial killings,” Massie said during a Monday press conference. “There’s no argument in these impeachment articles that he’s ineffective.”

Hegseth strongly pushed back against Massie’s salvo Tuesday morning at the Pentagon during his first press conference in more than six months, lambasting the Kentucky Republican as “one disgruntled and defeated congressman” who is following “a personal manifesto driven by ego and resentment.”

The Defense secretary told reporters Massie is attempting to “do damage to this president, this country, and most irresponsibly, the warriors who defend it” in his final days on Capitol Hill.

“It’s a farce, and it’s a stunt, and everybody knows it. In the 250 years of our American republic, no secretary of War or secretary of Defense has ever been impeached for carrying out lawful military operations, and in our case, successful ones at that,” Hegseth said during the press briefing, referring to the administration’s preferred name for the Defense Department.

Trump, Vice President Vance and other top administration officials stood behind Hegseth, panning the impeachment effort as “absurd” and praising Hegseth for his leadership at the Pentagon. Trump gave Hegseth an A-plus grade after his Tuesday morning press conference.

Several House Republicans put out statements in the lead-up to the vote offering support for the Defense secretary, noting he restored military readiness, executed Trump’s national security priorities and oversaw “critical reforms” at the Pentagon.

“The effort to impeach him is nothing more than petty, personal and partisan politics,” Rep. Ken Calvert (R-Calif.), the chair of the House Appropriations Subcommittee on Defense, said ahead of the vote. “Congress should focus on real threats to America and supporting our men and women in uniform by passing our appropriations bills instead of wasting time on impeachment proceedings.”

At the same time, Hegseth press aides took to the social platform X on Tuesday to push back on House Democrats ’ criticism of the Pentagon chief, highlighting the jump in recruitment numbers across all service branches, the lethal U.S. military strikes against alleged drug-trafficking boats in the Caribbean and Eastern Pacific, taking out ISIS global leader Abu-Bilal al-Minuki and other ISIS fighters in Africa and increasing pay for troops in hostile fire and imminent danger.

“We destroyed terror regimes’ capabilities, we sank the boats carrying poison into our communities, we put a narco-dictator in handcuffs,” Hegseth said Tuesday morning. “These are not high crimes. This is the job, and it’s a job well done.”

Heading into the vote, top Democratic leaders, including House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries (D-N.Y.), had announced their support for Massie’s resolution. But they did not pressure rank-and-file members to do the same, saying it was a vote of conscience for each lawmaker.

“We didn’t put our fingers on the scale,” said Rep. Pete Aguilar (D-Calif.), the outgoing chair of the House Democratic Caucus.

Aguilar, who’s in line to become the majority whip in the next Congress, also played down the idea that Democrats would race to try to impeach Hegseth again in the next Congress when they control the gavels.

“When we are in the majority, we are serious about holding people accountable, and that will … start early with oversight,” Aguilar said. “But that is not anything that is being discussed at this point.”

articles.title: Justiça determina despejo de lutador que agrediu vizinhas no Rio | G1
articles.standfirst: O despejo foi determinado pela 44ª Vara Cível da Capital, em uma ação movida pelos proprietários do apartamento.
articles.summary: A Justiça do Rio deu 15 dias para que Lucas Portela Fontana Gomes desocupe o apartamento no Maracanã após o lutador ser preso por agredir duas mulheres no prédio.
articles.body:
A Justiça do Rio determinou que Lucas Portela Fontana Gomes, preso por agredir duas mulheres em um condomínio no Maracanã , na Zona Norte do Rio, desocupe o apartamento onde mora no prazo de 15 dias. Ele está preso preventivamente.

O despejo foi determinado pela 44ª Vara Cível da Capital, em uma ação movida pelos proprietários do apartamento. Os locadores alegaram que as agressões praticadas pelo inquilino contra moradoras do prédio, no dia 5 de novembro, configuraram uma infração grave ao contrato de aluguel e às regras de convivência do condomínio.

Ao analisar o pedido, o juiz Antonio Luiz da Fonseca Lucchese considerou que havia elementos para conceder a tutela de urgência. Na decisão, ele afirmou que os relatos apresentados descrevem atos de violência que teriam incluído a invasão de um apartamento vizinho, agressões físicas e ameaças.

O magistrado destacou que as vítimas moram no mesmo edifício que o lutador e que uma eventual liberdade dele poderia permitir o retorno ao imóvel, colocando novamente as mulheres em situação de proximidade com Lucas.

A decisão afirma que esse cenário representa risco à integridade física, à segurança e à tranquilidade das moradoras.

O juiz determinou que a desocupação seja feita por uma pessoa previamente identificada, no prazo de 15 dias. Caso isso não aconteça voluntariamente, um oficial de justiça deverá cumprir o despejo compulsório, com autorização para uso de força policial e arrombamento, se necessário.

Os proprietários também foram autorizados a ficar como depositários dos bens que eventualmente forem deixados no apartamento.

Neste fim de semana, a Justiça converteu a prisão temporária de Lucas em preventiva . O homem está encarcerado na Cadeia Pública José Frederico Marques, em Benfica, na Zona Norte do Rio de Janeiro .

O lutador de jiu-jítsu Lucas Portela Fontana Gomes é faixa-marrom no esporte. A graduação é a penúltima antes da faixa-preta, considerada o nível mais alto da modalidade.

Segundo o professor Vinicius Kioto, praticantes do esporte aprendem desde o início que as técnicas de combate devem ser utilizadas para defesa pessoal, disciplina e esporte, nunca para iniciar agressões.

Kioto afirmou que a conduta atribuída ao lutador foge completamente dos princípios ensinados nas academias. Para ele, o conhecimento adquirido no tatame também traz a responsabilidade de saber quando não utilizar a força.

“O jiu-jítsu te dá autoconfiança, sabedoria de que você pode conseguir neutralizar uma pessoa, mas que você só deve fazer quando for em caso de defesa pessoal. Nunca para utilizar essa ferramenta, que é o jiu-jítsu, para agredir alguém, principalmente pessoas em situações mais vulneráveis que ele”, afirmou.

O professor também chamou atenção para a gravidade das técnicas que, segundo ele, foram utilizadas nas agressões. Kioto mencionou o mata-leão, golpe de estrangulamento que pode provocar consequências graves quando aplicado por tempo prolongado.

“São golpes muito contundentes. Inclusive, ele fez o golpe chamado mata-leão, no qual enforcou durante muito tempo, correndo risco até de causar um óbito da pessoa. Graças a Deus não foi esse o fim”, disse.

Para o instrutor, comportamentos agressivos como o atribuído a Lucas são incompatíveis com a prática da arte marcial. Ele afirmou que professores costumam afastar alunos que apresentam esse tipo de conduta.

“Geralmente, um atleta com esse comportamento não fica em nenhuma academia durante muito tempo, porque os professores logo expulsam ele da academia por não ser um comportamento típico de lutador de jiu-jítsu”, declarou.

Lucas foi expulso de uma academia de artes marciais há 1 ano por mau comportamento .

A TV Globo conversou com um professor de jiu-jítsu de Lucas. “Fiquei perplexo e profundamente triste com o que aconteceu. As imagens divulgadas são muito fortes e causam indignação. Nenhuma mulher deveria passar por uma situação tão brutal e traumática”, declarou o faixa-preta.

Lucas Portela Fontana Gomes — Foto: Reprodução

O docente falou da passagem de Lucas pelo estabelecimento. “Quando chegou [à academia], Lucas era bastante reservado. Com o passar do tempo, tornou-se mais comunicativo e sociável”, lembrou.

“Posteriormente, comecei a observar algumas atitudes incompatíveis com o ambiente esportivo que procuro manter, especialmente dificuldades em lidar com derrotas durante os treinos , acompanhadas de reações agressivas ”, prosseguiu.

“Conversei com ele, mas, diante da repetição de determinados comportamentos, entendi que não deveria continuar fazendo parte da equipe . Tomei essa decisão há mais ou menos 1 ano e, desde então, não mantive mais contato com ele”, destacou.

Ele ressaltou que não houve, no período em que Lucas treinou na academia, relatos de alunas sobre situações de assédio ou violência praticadas pelo preso. “Se tivesse recebido uma comunicação dessa natureza, teria adotado as providências cabíveis, com a seriedade e a responsabilidade que a situação exigiria.”

Ainda segundo o faixa-preta, Lucas “nunca participou de competições pela equipe nem teve trajetória como atleta de competição”.

“Como professor, procuro ensinar aos meus alunos que o jiu-jítsu vai muito além de técnicas de luta . É uma ferramenta de disciplina, respeito ao próximo, autocontrole e desenvolvimento humano . A violência contra uma mulher representa justamente o oposto de tudo aquilo em que acredito e procuro transmitir por meio do esporte”, afirmou.

Presidente da Federação de Jiu-jítsu, bicampeão de MMA e multicampeão de Jiu-jítsu e comentarista do canal Combate, Dudu Dantas chama a atenção para a formação dos professores.

"Precisamos formar educadores e referências, pessoas conscientes do impacto que causam sobre seus alunos e sobre a sociedade. O Código Marcial nasceu para contribuir com essa formação: preparar instrutores para ensinar com mais responsabilidade, conhecimento e compromisso com as pessoas que confiam neles".

"O jiu-jitsu é chamado de arte suave. Nasceu para que o mais fraco possa se defender do mais forte. Quando alguém usa a técnica para o contrário, vai contra tudo o que construímos. Conheço o poder que o treino dá a um atleta. E sei que, quanto maior a nossa capacidade de causar dano, maior tem de ser a nossa responsabilidade de nunca usá-la para agredir alguém. Não existe honra, disciplina ou respeito quando a força serve para intimidar, humilhar ou machucar uma pessoa", acrescentou.

Lucas Portela Fontana Gomes agride vizinha no elevador — Foto: Reprodução

Na audiência de custódia que manteve a prisão, Lucas afirmou que é usuário de maconha, cocaína, quetamina e remédios controlados . Ele já tinha afirmado em depoimento à polícia que também usa anabolizantes.

A defesa do lutador afirmou que os ataques foram “uma reação grave ao uso de medicamentos controlados” . No entanto, não foi realizado exame toxicológico para determinar se ele estava sob efeito de alguma substância.

O juiz ainda escreveu na ata que Lucas não aparentava ter nenhum transtorno mental .

articles.title: A farmer's son watched his village's fortunes depend on farming; today, his Namakkal software company has 26 employees, clients in seven countries and Rs 1.5 crore in annual project revenue
articles.summary: Eswaran Arumugam’s father was a farmer.
articles.body: Eswaran Arumugam’s father was a farmer. But he chose to build a software company that today has clients in several nations and has crores worth annual project revenue. It was an unlikely ambition for someone who comes from an agricultural background. But Arumugam, founder of Yaa Creations, has shown that a technology business need not begin in a metropolitan city to find a place to go internationally.As reported in an interview with YourStory, his company, based in Rasipuram in Tamil Nadu's Namakkal district, has grown from a one-person venture into a 26-member team that serves clients across seven countries and undertook projects worth Rs 1.5 crore in 2025.The inspirational journey of EswaranEswaran's journey started in a small village named Pallipatti in Namakkal district. He came from a modest middle-class family and grew up seeing his parents running a small grocery store. Education became an important part of the family's aspirations. While Eswaran pursued a Bachelor of Science degree followed by a Master of Computer Applications (MCA), his brothers also pursued higher education.His professional journey began in 2011 when he joined a Chennai-based software startup as a junior software developer. His starting salary was Rs 3,500 a month.He worked with the company for nine years and started taking on greater responsibilities and became a technical lead. Those years shaped his ambition of creating his own software, understanding client requirements and managing technology projects.However, health-related difficulties eventually prompted him to leave Chennai and return to his hometown. What initially appeared to be an interruption in his career became the starting point of a new venture.Starting with Rs 1 lakh and two laptopsThe idea of establishing a software company emerged during conversations with his brothers. Eswaran had the technical experience, but starting a business required money.When he received a small software development project, he decided to take a chance. He borrowed Rs 1 lakh from his brother, returned to Chennai, rented a co-working space for Rs 10,000 a month and purchased two laptops.He named the venture Yaa Creations. The beginning, however, was far from smooth. He hired a woman software developer at a monthly salary of Rs 30,000 and managed to pay her salary and the office rent using the initial project payment and his remaining funds. But new orders did not come.To make the matter worse, the COVID-19 pandemic happened. With work drying up and operations disrupted, he had to return to his hometown. In February 2020, Eswaran restarted operations near his native village and hired two people. But lockdown-related disruptions affected the new venture as well.Financial pressure mounted. He eventually accumulated debts of around Rs 5 lakh while struggling to meet monthly expenses and keep the business operational. He had no money left to fulfill the basic needs of his kid.Taking every project that came his wayIt was the time when Eswaran decided to take every project that came to him. Its work covered website development, mobile applications, software solutions, surveys and digital services.The company's reported project earnings grew from Rs 3 lakh in its first year to Rs 7 lakh, followed by Rs 10 lakh and then Rs 30 lakh in subsequent years.Eswaran believes continuous learning has been central to this growth. The company has also expanded its capabilities to include advanced software products and mobile applications incorporating artificial intelligence technologies.From Rasipuram to international clientsThe company has reportedly worked with clients in countries including Sri Lanka, Singapore, Malaysia, Qatar and Germany, among others, and now serves seven countries.Its work has also extended to public-sector projects.One notable assignment involved a student survey for Tiruppur Municipal Corporation. The project focused on understanding the academic performance and educational choices of Class 10 and Class 12 students in government schools. Information about students' subject preferences, reasons for poor performance and plans for higher education was collected to help identify areas requiring attention.Another project involved Salem Medical College Hospital, where the company developed a QR-code-based identity system for patient attendants. The system was designed to record visitor details and monitor hospital entry and exit, helping improve identification and access management.From a modest beginning in Namakkal to projects spanning international markets, Yaa Creations' growth reflects what can happen when technical experience, persistence and a willingness to start small come together.You use AI every day. articles.title: Nvidia spy scandal could reshape fight over AI chips and China
articles.summary: Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang’s relationship with an alleged Chinese spy is putting a microscope on the company’s influence on AI chip policy in Washington and throwing new momentum behind a trio of bills aiming to place restrictions on chip sales abroad. Huang’s disclosure of his affair with a Chinese businessperson, who U.S. officials concluded was…
articles.body:
Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang’s relationship with an alleged Chinese spy is putting a microscope on the company’s influence on AI chip policy in Washington and throwing new momentum behind a trio of bills aiming to place restrictions on chip sales abroad.

Huang’s disclosure of his affair with a Chinese businessperson, who U.S. officials concluded was a Chinese intelligence asset, renewed attention on chips policy just as lawmakers returned to Washington this week to kick off the lame-duck session.

The explosive revelations are adding new fuel to a months-long push to include the legislation in a must-pass defense bill before the end of the year.

“NVIDIA’s CEO just confirmed a relationship with a suspected Chinese spy,” Sen. Elizabeth Warren (D-Mass.) wrote on the social platform X. “Congress is back today. We have legislation ready to go to stop advanced AI chips from fueling China’s military. Let’s get this done.”

Nvidia’s board of directors launched an investigation Sunday, after Huang said he had been “unfaithful” to his wife and appeared to confirm his affair with Alice Huang, an executive at the Singapore-based data center company Megaspeed who is suspected of passing information to Beijing.

The probe is set to focus on U.S. national and economic security, though the board said it did not have any reason to believe national security or company secrets were compromised.

The House Foreign Affairs Committee said on X the scandal is a “great example of why we need AI export control bills” to ensure “China can never get their hands on our most advanced technology.”

The incident could damage Jensen Huang’s credibility, and, in turn, his influence on Washington policies, chip export control advocates told The Hill.

The Nvidia chief became a powerful player in D.C. over the past two years, advocating for fewer restrictions on chip sales to China.

Jensen Huang argued that giving Beijing access to its third- or fourth-best chips could keep the country dependent on American-made infrastructure. His efforts paid off at times, as the Trump administration agreed to allow for sales of Nvidia’s H20 and H200 chips last year.

“The biggest threat to these bills was always that Jensen Huang used his political capital with the White House and even Congress to block them. And that obstacle just got blown up,” a lobbyist at an AI policy group told The Hill. “The percentage of these bills passing now are astronomically high.”

Lawmakers in favor of stricter export controls have long eyed the National Defense Authorization Act (NDAA) as a potential vehicle for multiple bills curbing China’s access to U.S.-made AI chips.

Over the summer, three chip export bills made it into the manager’s amendments for the NDAA, which still needs to pass through Congress by the end of the year.

The bills include the Artificial Intelligence Oversight of Verified Exports and Restrictions on Weaponizable Advanced Technology to Covered High-Risk Actors (AI Overwatch) Act, the Multilateral Alignment of Technology Controls on Hardware (MATCH) Act and the Chip Security Act.

The AI Overwatch Act , introduced by Warren and Sen. Jim Banks (R-Ind.), would allow Congress to block advanced AI chip exports to U.S. foreign adversaries.

The MATCH Act, introduced by Sens. Andy Kim (D-N.J.), James Risch (R-Idaho) and Pete Ricketts (R-Neb.), would block the sale of essential chipmaking tools to countries of concern.

The Chip Security Act, put forward by Sen. Tom Cotton (R-Ark.), would require AI chips subject to export controls to have a “location verification mechanism.”

“There were people advising the Administration that Communist China did not need or want our high-end chips. If these allegations are true that is clearly not the case,” Ricketts said in a statement Monday, calling for the passage of two chip-related measures.

“We need to know if Chinese spies received sensitive information and if Nvidia chips were illegally smuggled through Megaspeed,” he continued. “We need to stop Communist China from obtaining our high-end technology.”

House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries (D-N.Y.), who’s in line to become Speaker in the next Congress, told reporters Monday that Nvidia came up during a classified briefing on Iran, saying it’s clear there are “real concerns that need to be addressed.”

Jeffries also threw his weight behind the idea of restricting the export of high-value chips to China, saying he “strongly supports” the limits the Senate is pushing in its version of the NDAA.

“We’re going to work hard to make sure that those provisions make it into the final version” of the bill, he said.

In a sign it may be willing to play ball, the White House gave feedback on multiple chip exports bills, Punchbowl News reported.

This marks a shift from last year, when the Guaranteeing Access and Innovation for National Artificial Intelligence (GAIN AI) Act was stripped from the NDAA after pushback from the White House.

The GAIN AI Act, also put forward by Warren and Banks, would have required chipmakers to give U.S. firms first pick on advanced AI chips before selling to China or other countries of concern.

The scandal “adds impetus to the Democrats’ push to tighten up export controls,” said Sam Bresnick, a research fellow at Georgetown University’s Center for Security and Emerging Technology who focuses on national security applications of AI.

But it’s unclear whether this will be enough to push the chip bills over the finish line.

There is “a very open question as to how much they can actually get done from this messaging opportunity and how long any kind of momentum out of this remains,” noted Owen Tedford, a senior research analyst at Beacon Policy Advisors.

Despite touting bipartisan support, the latest push for the chip bills also comes at a moment when Congress’s annual Defense authorization bill is already on thin ice amid partisan infighting.

Investigations into Jensen Huang are likely to pick up as Democrats prepare to take control of both chambers of Congress next year.

Sen. Chris Coons (D-Del.), who is expected to be the chair of the Senate Foreign Relations Committee next year, said he is “pushing to investigate” Jensen Huang and Nvidia to determine whether national security was compromised.

“The Democrats are going to come in guns blazing on the issue in January,” Bresnick said.

The scrutiny is also coming from across the aisle.

A trio of top House GOP lawmakers — House Foreign Affairs Committee Chair Brian Mast (Fla.), House Select Committee on China Chair John Moolenaar (Mich.) and House Intelligence Committee Chair Rick Crawford (Ark.) — asked Jensen Huang on Thursday to appear for a closed-door briefing about the company’s security protocols.

articles.title: I asked every TV manufacturer 17 questions about how they spy on you
articles.summary: After LG was accused of spying through its TVs, I wanted to see how other TV companies were collecting and protecting our data.﻿
articles.body: Every TV company is spying on you, not just LG. Like other tech companies, they collect lots of information, and while some is necessary for products to work, not all of it is — and could include details you’d prefer to keep private. Many customers are concerned about how TVs and streaming devices might be spying: listening to what you say, taking screenshots of everything you watch, storing sensitive information on your TV, and sharing your data with the cloud. To find out what TV and streaming device companies are doing, I decided to ask every one to explain itself. I put together 17 yes-or-no questions, like “Do your TVs store any recorded audio, or transcripts based on audio, captured in the home?” so that companies couldn’t just link to a confusing and legalese-ridden privacy policy. TV users deserve to know the answers. --- Company representatives providing responses Amazon: Eric Sveum, PR manager Apple: Emily Ewing, public relations manager Google: Alex García-Kummert, spokesperson LG Electronics: Chris De Maria, director of public relations Roku: Sarah Novatt, spokesperson Samsung: Frank Giancamilli, corporate communications senior manager TCL: Rob Manfredo, head of communications and events --- One month ago, I invited 11 companies, including Amazon, Apple, Google, Hisense, LG, Panasonic, Roku, Samsung, Sony, TCL, and Walmart’s Vizio to share those answers. We now have answers from the top three TV manufacturers as well as every major streaming device company. Some companies declined to answer. Below, you can see and compare how each company answered (or failed to answer) each question and then decide how you feel. (One company, Hisense, ignored our emails entirely.) As you’ll see them say, some of this data collection is opt-in, and you can often opt out. We know that many TVs use automatic content recognition (ACR) to figure out potentially everything we’re watching, and use that information to tailor ads, gather audience metrics, and serve up content recommendations based on our viewing habits. But though it sometimes seems like it’s required during the cavalcade of agreements thrown at us during setup, you can generally stop ACR even after you’ve agreed to it. Opting out might not be as effective as it should be, however. A recent Northeastern University study found that Walmart’s Vizio kept on sending data after an opt-out (Vizio told me it was “routine operational data used to support the Vizio experience,” not ACR), while traffic with both Samsung and Roku was limited, but not stopped completely. Below are the answers to our 17 questions. You will notice that some companies would not answer yes or no. We’ve also noted where companies declined to answer at all or ignored the questions. If any company becomes willing to directly answer our questions, we’ll add their responses. 1. Do your TVs ever use their embedded microphones, or the microphones in their remotes, to listen to sound in a customer’s home? Amazon: > No. Fire TV includes voice functionality to help customers use their devices and get to content they love and fast, not to surveil homes. The microphones on our voice remotes are designed to only work when the mic button on the remote is physically pressed. And TVs with hands-free Alexa are designed to detect the wake word (and only the wake word) before connecting to Alexa. No audio is stored or sent to the cloud unless the device detects the wake word. Customers can also turn off the microphones at any time. Every Fire TV smart television that has microphones also has a physical button or switch that disables the microphone. Apple: > Apple TV 4K will use its far-field microphones and the Always On Processor strictly to listen for the Siri wake word. The Always On Processor does not process or act on any other sounds in the home. Users have full control over this and can turn off “Siri” or “Hey Siri” as a wake word, or disable Siri entirely. When using the Siri Remote, users must actively press and hold the microphone button for it to start listening. Google: > If Google Assistant or Gemini is enabled or available, microphones (built-in hands-free ‘Hey Google’ or remote push-to-talk button) listen for activation triggers. Microphones remain in passive standby until triggered by hotword or button press. Hisense: Hisense did not respond to The Verge’s questions despite five attempts to make contact. LG: > Voice recognition is off by default and operates only if the user has opted in by accepting the Voice Information Agreement. Even if the user has opted in, they need to take additional steps for the microphone to be used. They must either press the microphone button on the remote control or they can use Hands-free Voice Control on supported models. > Hands-free Voice Control is disabled unless a user opts into this feature and then uses a wake-word. Wake-word detection is performed locally on the TV. If no wake word is detected, the audio is processed locally, promptly deleted, and is not stored, converted to text, or transmitted. Panasonic: Panasonic did not provide an answer to this question. Roku: > While Roku TVs don’t have built-in microphones, some Roku remotes do. Standard voice remotes listen only while the mic button is held, and hands-free remotes can be switched off. Samsung: > No, for private monitoring. Samsung TVs do not listen to or record private conversations. > The TV’s embedded microphone only listens locally for the specific wake-up word (like “Hi, Bixby”) and ignores all other sounds, while the remote control microphone only activates when the customer physically presses the button. Sony: Sony did not provide an answer to this question. TCL: > Some TCL TVs and remotes have microphones. Users can activate those microphones to use voice assistance features provided through third-party operating systems or applications. Those third parties control whether the voice features are available and how they are used, under their own terms and privacy policies. Vizio: Vizio did not provide an answer to this question. 2. Do your TVs store any recorded audio, or transcripts based on audio, captured in the home? Amazon: > No. Apple: Apple did not provide a direct answer to this question. Google: > [Recorded audio and/or transcripts based on audio are] stored only if ‘Voice & Audio Activity’ (VAA) is explicitly enabled under Google Account Web & App Activity. Voice & Audio Activity is off by default. If VAA is off, voice requests are processed in real-time and not saved to the Google Account. Hisense: Hisense did not respond to The Verge’s questions despite five attempts to make contact. LG: > If voice recognition is enabled (by opting in) and activated (by pushing the remote control’s microphone button or using the wake word), certain information generated as part of a specific voice recognition interaction may be stored locally on the TV to support voice-related features. Depending on the interaction, this may include Speech-to-text results derived from a user’s voice command. > Audio used for wake-word detection is processed locally on the TV and, if no wake word is detected, captured audio is promptly deleted, and is not stored, converted to text, or transmitted. Panasonic: Panasonic did not provide an answer to this question. Roku: > Voice commands made via voice-enabled remotes may be retained to improve voice features and provide support, consistent with Roku’s privacy policy. Users can opt out in their Roku account privacy settings. Samsung: > No. Samsung Smart TVs do not store voice recordings or transcripts on the device. > However, on secure servers, voice commands and transcripts are stored only to process requests and improve voice assistant services. Sony: Sony did not provide an answer to this question. TCL: > TCL does not collect audio data from TCL TV or remote microphones, or from the use of third-party voice features. Vizio: Vizio did not provide an answer to this question. 3. Do your TVs transmit any audio, or transcripts based on audio, captured in the home? Amazon: > When customers speak to Alexa by pressing the mic button on the remote or using their chosen wake word, a recording of the request is sent to Amazon’s cloud, where a text transcript of the request is created to help Alexa provide a response. No audio is captured without the customer invoking Alexa—either by pressing the mic button or saying the wake word—and customers can easily review exactly what they asked and what Alexa heard, delete their recording, or even choose not to save them at all. Apple: > Siri AI processes user requests using on-device processing, and when a request needs more powerful AI models, it extends those same on-device privacy protections to the cloud through a groundbreaking infrastructure called Private Cloud Compute (PCC). When Private Cloud Compute is handling users’ requests, their personal data is not stored nor made accessible to Apple, or anyone else, and outside experts can verify this privacy promise at any time. > For moments when users ask a question that requires up‑to‑date information, Siri AI can go out to the web and find it, then use Private Cloud Compute to generate an answer. Searches and requests are associated with a random identifier — a long string of letters and numbers — not a user’s Apple Account. Google: > If Voice & Audio Activity is turned on, when voice features are activated (via hotword or remote button), captured audio or transcripts are transmitted to Google cloud servers for processing and fulfilling commands. If VAA is turned off, these are deleted. Hisense: Hisense did not respond to The Verge’s questions despite five attempts to make contact. LG: > Yes, but only if voice recognition has been enabled (by opting in) and activated (by pushing the remote control microphone button or using the wake word). When voice recognition is activated, the TV displays an on-screen indication that voice recognition is active and listening for the user’s command. Once the user finishes the voice command, the command is transmitted to our server, where it is converted into text and processed to respond to the command. Panasonic: Panasonic did not provide an answer to this question. Roku: > Roku TVs don’t have microphones. Voice-enabled remotes let people control their Roku devices by voice, as described in our privacy policy. Samsung: > No, for ambient or background listening. Samsung TVs do not passively monitor, record, or transmit audio from your home. Audio is only captured and transmitted when you actively initiate a voice command (such as pressing the microphone button on your remote or using the wake word). This voice input is processed securely to fulfill your requests, improve services, and support connected features under our voice privacy policies. Sony: Sony did not provide an answer to this question. TCL: TCL did not provide a direct answer to this question. Vizio: Vizio did not provide an answer to this question. 4. Do your TVs collect any screenshots, screen recordings, or video recordings of what viewers are watching? Amazon: > No. Apple: > Apple TV 4K does not use automatic content recognition (ACR), nor does it collect screenshots, screen recordings, or video recordings of what viewers are watching. If a user chooses to ask a question about what’s on their screen, that data is processed by Siri AI. This feature is only initiated by a direct user request. Google: > Google TV platform software does not utilize Automatic Content Recognition (ACR) to capture on-screen video or screenshots. (Note: Third-party TV hardware OEMs may install separate ACR software, but Google TV OS itself does not). Hisense: Hisense did not respond to The Verge’s questions despite five attempts to make contact. LG: > No. ACR in LG TVs does not collect or store screenshots, screen images, screen recordings, or video recordings from the TV. Instead, it uses audio fingerprints generated from content audio using the TV’s internal soundboard (not a speaker) to identify the content being viewed. Panasonic: Panasonic did not provide an answer to this question. Roku: > No. Samsung: > No. Samsung TVs do not capture or store screenshots, screen recordings, or video recordings of what viewers watch. Sony: Sony did not provide an answer to this question. TCL: TCL did not provide a direct answer to this question. Vizio: Vizio did not provide an answer to this question. 5. Do your TVs store or transmit data on what content viewers watch or listen to through the TV? Amazon: > Yes. For example, customers can opt in to allow Fire TV to collect certain viewing information like what shows they’ve watched in third-party apps to improve and personalize their experience, including by displaying shows and movies in a Continue Watching row on the Fire TV home screen. Customers can manage that setting anytime via their device’s Privacy Settings. Apple: Apple did not provide a direct answer to this question. Google: > [Google TV] stores and transmits viewing history, watchlists, and app interactions for rentals/purchases on GTV and FreePlay. We do not have viewing history on third party apps. Hisense: Hisense did not respond to The Verge’s questions despite five attempts to make contact. LG: > If the user has agreed to the Viewing Information Agreement, viewing information may be collected or processed in certain circumstances, including the following: > - ACR: Where ACR is available and enabled, ACR-related information may be collected and processed to identify content being viewed from supported sources. ACR uses audio fingerprinting technology to identify content rather than collecting screenshots, screen recordings, video recordings, voice recordings, or other audio recordings from the TV. To operate ACR services, LG may process content-identification fingerprints together with device information, content source information, network information, and consent settings needed to support the feature. ACR is optional and is turned off by default, and users can disable the feature at any time through the TV settings. ACR does not operate within third-party streaming apps. > - LG Channels: When a user streams content through LG Channels, information about the content being viewed is processed and sent to our servers so we can provide the requested streaming service. > - Voice Recognition: When users make voice commands, those commands and current viewing information (such as channel number and program name, and whether the source is an antenna or set-top-box) are sent to the server to process the voice commands and provide appropriate responses. > - Usage Information: Certain viewing information may also be collected as part of usage information relating to how the user interacts with the TV and its services, such as information about content selected for viewing or channels the user switches to. Panasonic: Panasonic did not provide an answer to this question. Roku: > We collect streaming activity as described in our privacy policy. Smart TV Experience, which can identify other content on screen, is off by default in the US and is enabled only if the user opts in. Samsung: > Yes, but only for TV programming and app viewing history. Samsung TVs do not monitor or transmit your personal files or private media. Sony: Sony did not provide an answer to this question. TCL: > TCL collects limited data only for diagnostics and product improvement from some models of TCL Smart TVs. This collection is disclosed to users at setup and in TCL’s privacy notice, uses pseudonymization to prevent user profiling, and can be turned off by the user. Vizio: Vizio did not provide an answer to this question. 6. Do your TVs collect any telemetry about where users are clicking, selecting, tapping, or otherwise looking when using the TV? Amazon: > Fire TV collects data about how customers use the device, such as navigating the home screen or opening apps, to provide and improve features. Customers can opt out of certain data collection and use via Privacy Settings. Apple: Apple did not provide an answer to this question. Google: > [Google TV] collects device navigation telemetry (button presses, navigation clicks, app launch/exit events) under ‘Usage & Diagnostics’ settings to assess system health and reliability. Does not store “hovering” or “highlight” states. Hisense: Hisense did not respond to The Verge’s questions despite five attempts to make contact. LG: > To provide and improve smart services, the LG smart TV may collect certain basic usage information about how users interact with the TV, such as the features, menu items, apps, or services they select or use. LG does not collect information about a user’s activity within third-party apps. LG does not track where users are looking when using the TV. Panasonic: Panasonic did not provide an answer to this question. Roku: > We collect standard usage data, such as button presses and menu selections, to run and improve the product. Samsung: > For menu interactions and viewing selections, interactions (like clicks or selections) are analyzed primarily in aggregate to improve the user experience and service recommendations. Sony: Sony did not provide an answer to this question. TCL: > TCL does not collect data at the device level regarding what viewers watch, except when a user requests remote diagnostic support, in which case the information is used to fix the problem the user reported. Vizio: Vizio did not provide an answer to this question. 7. Do your TVs transmit any information that could identify the location of their owner, including their public IP address, Wi-Fi network SSID, GPS coordinates, and/or actual street address? Amazon: > Yes. For example, IP addresses are transmitted as part of normal network communication, for your device to communicate with the internet and deliver content. There is no GPS hardware on Fire TV devices. Apple: Apple did not provide a direct answer to this question. Google: > [Google TV] transmits public IP address, Wi-Fi scan data (SSID/BSSID), and account/device regional configuration to determine approximate or precise device location. Hisense: Hisense did not respond to The Verge’s questions despite five attempts to make contact. LG: > To provide Smart TV functionality, the TV must be connected to the internet. If the TV is connected to the internet, then like any other internet-connected device, the Smart TV will transmit its IP address. The IP address may be used to determine its approximate geographic location to provide services appropriate for the user’s region. > Separately, when ACR is enabled, the TV’s IP address and information about nearby Wi-Fi networks, such as MAC addresses and signal strength, may be used to estimate the TV’s approximate location as part of the ACR service. This ACR-related location processing is limited to ACR and is not used generally across other TV services. > The TV does not contain a GPS module and does not use GPS to determine its location. Panasonic: Panasonic did not provide an answer to this question. Roku: > Roku TVs don’t collect GPS data. Like any connected device, they transmit a public IP address, which may be used for approximate location, among other purposes, per our privacy policy. Samsung: > No, for physical locations. Samsung TVs do not collect or transmit GPS coordinates, Wi-Fi SSIDs, or your physical street address. However, for network connection, the TV must transmit its public IP address to connect to the internet and run basic features (like the Smart Hub and software updates). This IP address is only used for network communication and general region detection (like country or state), not to pinpoint your actual address. Sony: Sony did not provide an answer to this question. TCL: > To provide location-based services, TCL collects IP address and Wi-Fi network name (SSID) information, as described in the terms and privacy policy to which users agree when they initially set up their TV. TCL uses this information only to identify a country or city in order to deliver services, not the user’s specific location. TCL TVs have no GPS modules, and TCL does not collect street addresses through the TV. If a user creates a TCL account on a TCL Google TV, TCL collects an email address and age to confirm that the user is an adult. Apart from that, TCL’s practice is not to collect personally identifiable information from its televisions. Vizio: Vizio did not provide an answer to this question. 8. Do your TVs store or transmit any other potentially personally identifying information about their owners, including their name, age, gender, orientation, and demographic? Amazon: > Fire TV devices are associated with customers’ Amazon account, which includes their name and account information. Apple: Apple did not provide an answer to this question. Google: > Because Google TV requires a Google Account for smart functionality, linked profile information (name, email, age, gender) is accessed, stored, and transmitted for personalization and age-restriction policies. Hisense: Hisense did not respond to The Verge’s questions despite five attempts to make contact. LG: > When creating an LG account, the user provides their name, email address and date of birth (to confirm applicable age requirements). If a user creates an LG account from their Smart TV, the TV will temporarily store and then transmit this information to LG’s servers. Panasonic: Panasonic did not provide an answer to this question. Roku: > Users provide account information, such as name and email, when they create a Roku account, as described in our privacy policy. Samsung: > Samsung SmartTVs do not collect/store or transmit name, age, gender, orientation or demographic information. Sony: Sony did not provide an answer to this question. TCL: > If a user creates a TCL account on a TCL Google TV, TCL collects an email address and age to confirm that the user is an adult. Apart from that, TCL’s practice is not to collect personally identifiable information from its televisions. Vizio: Vizio did not provide an answer to this question. 9. Does your company store any of the kinds of information in Question 7 or 8 in the cloud or other remote servers? If so, which? Amazon: > Yes. Information transmitted to Amazon’s cloud is encrypted in transit and stored securely. Apple: Apple did not provide an answer to this question. Google: > Both location data (IP address/Wi-Fi) and Google Account profile data (name, email address, age/gender demographics) are stored on Google’s cloud servers linked to your account profile. Hisense: Hisense did not respond to The Verge’s questions despite five attempts to make contact. LG: > Yes. Information such as IP addresses, device-level identifiers, and, if a user has an LG Account, account information such as name, email address, and date of birth, is stored on LG’s cloud or other remote servers. When ACR is enabled, the ACR-related information described above, including nearby Wi-Fi network information such as MAC addresses and signal strength, may also be stored on remote servers. Panasonic: Panasonic did not provide an answer to this question. Roku: > Data may be stored on Roku’s servers or with major cloud providers to operate the service, as described in our privacy policy. Samsung: > Yes. The information described above is stored in encrypted or hashed form within secure cloud infrastructure managed by Samsung. Sony: Sony did not provide an answer to this question. TCL: > The limited information described above is stored with cloud service providers, including Amazon Web Services, Microsoft Azure, and Google Cloud, subject to TCL’s terms and privacy policy. Vizio: Vizio did not provide an answer to this question. 10. Do your TVs transmit any information about the other devices on an owner’s home Wi-Fi network? Amazon: > No. Apple: Apple did not provide an answer to this question. Google: > [Google TV] discovers nearby Cast-enabled devices and smart home hardware via local network protocols (mDNS, SSDP, Matter/Thread) and transmits device discovery/connectivity logs. Hisense: Hisense did not respond to The Verge’s questions despite five attempts to make contact. LG: > To support connectivity capabilities, LG smart TVs identify other devices on the user’s Wi-Fi network. Where necessary to support device-discovery functionality, information about nearby devices detected on the local network may be transmitted to a third-party service provider acting on LG’s behalf to identify compatible devices. Panasonic: Panasonic did not provide an answer to this question. Roku: > Roku TVs may detect other devices on the home network to support features like AirPlay, as described in our privacy policy. Samsung: > No. Samsung TVs do not scan your home Wi-Fi network to collect or transmit an inventory of other connected devices. The TV only communicates with compatible devices that customers actively choose to connect (such as for casting or via the SmartThings app under their Samsung Account) to provide smart home control, not to monitor other devices on your network. Sony: Sony did not provide an answer to this question. TCL: > Users may connect their TCL Smart TV to other devices so they can control those devices. For some on-device functions, such as screen casting or connecting devices to each other, the TV may detect other devices on the same Wi-Fi network. That data is normally exchanged only between the devices. If a connection problem occurs, diagnostics may report the name of the device involved. When a consumer chooses to control the TV through a voice service such as Amazon Alexa, data is exchanged between the TV, TCL’s cloud, and Amazon so the service can function. Vizio: Vizio did not provide an answer to this question. 11. Can users entirely opt out of transmitting all forms of data? Amazon: > No. Basic functionality like downloading apps and streaming content requires transmitting data. However, Fire TV does provide customers the ability to control the collection or transmission of certain data, including data about the frequency and duration of use of third-party apps and about what customers have watched in third-party apps. Apple: Apple did not provide an answer to this question. Google: > Users cannot opt out of 100% of data transmission while connected to the internet. Essential system telemetry (device model, OS version, activation status, security updates) is mandatory for basic operation. Hisense: Hisense did not respond to The Verge’s questions despite five attempts to make contact. LG: > Users can stop the transmission of personal data associated with smart TV services by withdrawing their acceptance of the Privacy Policy or Terms of Use. If they do so, smart TV services will no longer be available, and the data transmission required to provide those services will cease. The TV can still be used for basic functions that do not require smart TV services, such as Live TV or HDMI inputs. > Users can also separately choose whether to use optional features such as voice recognition, ACR, and interest-based advertising. These features require separate agreements and can be reviewed, managed, or withdrawn through the TV settings at any time. Declining or withdrawing these optional agreements does not prevent users from using core smart TV functionality. Panasonic: Panasonic did not provide an answer to this question. Roku: > No, but Roku offers privacy settings for voice data, Smart TV Experience, and ad personalization. Samsung: > No, not all forms. At minimum, data is needed to run a digital platform (e.g. to provide the service and security). Sony: Sony did not provide an answer to this question. TCL: > Some data is transmitted to TCL because the Smart TV services and functions the user chooses depend on such data. Users can opt out of sending TCL the limited interaction data collected for diagnostics and product improvement. Vizio: Vizio did not provide an answer to this question. 12. Are users automatically opted out by default when setting up the TV? Amazon: > Customers are not opted out of all data transmission by default. Again, basic device functionality requires data to be transmitted. However, there are some Fire TV features like Automatic Content Recognition that are default off and that customers must affirmatively turn on in order to allow those features to work and transmit data. Apple: Apple did not provide an answer to this question. Google: > During initial setup, options such as Usage & Diagnostics sharing, personalized recommendations/ads, and Google Account Web & App Activity tracking are enabled by default unless opted out. Hisense: Hisense did not respond to The Verge’s questions despite five attempts to make contact. LG: > Yes. Users can choose to opt-in by accepting each applicable agreement before the relevant services or features are enabled. Optional features such as voice recognition, ACR, and interest-based advertising are not enabled by default . Users can also manage or withdraw their consent through the TV settings at any time. Panasonic: Panasonic did not provide an answer to this question. Roku: > Smart TV Experience is off by default in the US. Samsung: > Yes. For Viewing Information Services (VIS), which includes Automatic Content Recognition (ACR), consumers are opted out by default and must affirmatively enable it. Sony: Sony did not provide an answer to this question. TCL: > Users can opt out of sending TCL the limited interaction data collected for diagnostics and product improvement. > The ACR technology on those TCL Smart TVs which support that feature comes from the operating system provider or third-party software providers. Users choose whether to turn on ACR when they first set up the TV, and they can turn it off at any time in the ACR provider’s privacy settings. Before ACR is turned on, the user must agree to the ACR provider’s terms and conditions. Those terms and privacy policies explain what viewing data the provider may store or transmit with the user’s consent. Vizio: Vizio did not provide an answer to this question. 13. If users opt out, does the TV store any of these forms of data internally for potential use at a later date? Amazon: > No. If a customer has opted out of Fire TV collecting data, that data will not be collected unless the customer re-enables collection. Apple: Apple did not provide an answer to this question. Google: > If cloud tracking is disabled, local temporary caches and system operational buffers remain on-device for immediate system execution and local performance before deletion. Hisense: Hisense did not respond to The Verge’s questions despite five attempts to make contact. LG: > No. If a user withdraws consent under an applicable agreement, data previously collected under that agreement is handled in accordance with LG’s applicable data retention and deletion policies, including deletion or anonymization where appropriate, and is not retained for potential future use. Panasonic: Panasonic did not provide an answer to this question. Roku: > Roku’s ad personalization setting affects which ads users see. Data is still collected and used for other purposes, as described in our privacy policy. Samsung: > No. If users opt out, the TV stops collecting new viewing data immediately and does not store it internally for later use. Once you disable the Viewing Information Services (VIS), any previously collected ACR data is deleted from our servers and can no longer be associated with your device. Sony: Sony did not provide an answer to this question. TCL: TCL did not provide a direct answer to this question. Vizio: Vizio did not provide an answer to this question. 14. Does disconnecting a TV from the internet prevent all these forms of data transmission? Amazon: > Yes. Apple: Apple did not provide an answer to this question. Of course this also stops any streaming service from operating. Hisense: Hisense did not respond to The Verge’s questions despite five attempts to make contact. LG: > Yes. A TV must be connected to the internet to transmit data. For voice recognition specifically, voice data is not stored for later upload when the TV is offline and is not transmitted when the connection is restored. Amazon: > Yes, smart TVs will store some data locally to transmit once connectivity has been re-established. For example, if an application were to crash while your smart TV was offline, the device might store that data locally to be able to transmit it once connectivity has been reestablished—for the purpose of ensuring your devices and services are working as they should. Apple: Apple did not provide an answer to this question. For example, voice recognition data is not stored for later upload while the TV is offline and is not subsequently transmitted when the internet connection is restored. Panasonic: Panasonic did not provide an answer to this question. Roku: > Some usage data may be briefly held on the device until the connection returns or the device is turned off. Samsung: > Yes, but is dependent upon what features are enabled on the TV and the model year of the device. Sony: Sony did not provide an answer to this question. TCL: > Unless a consumer has opted out, the TV stores certain diagnostic and performance data while offline, which is processed once the TV reconnects. Vizio: Vizio did not provide an answer to this question. 16. Is collected data encrypted on device? Is it encrypted in transit? Is it encrypted end-to-end? Amazon: > Data is encrypted in transit. Apple: Apple did not provide an answer to this question. Google: > On-device: YES (Android file-based encryption). In transit: YES (TLS/HTTPS). End-to-end: NO for standard queries/telemetry, as Google servers must decrypt requests to process voice commands and content recommendations. Hisense: Hisense did not respond to The Verge’s questions despite five attempts to make contact. LG: > Personal information, such as LG Account information, is encrypted. Other information, such as STT results, may be stored without encryption. All data transmitted from the device to the server is sent through an encrypted channel. Panasonic: Panasonic did not provide an answer to this question. Roku: > Roku uses industry-standard security measures to protect data, specifically end-to-end encryption. Samsung: > Yes. Automatic Content Recognition (ACR) information collected by Samsung TVs is hashed for privacy, and is encrypted in transit and at storage. Sony: Sony did not provide an answer to this question. TCL: > Data collected by TCL is encrypted in transit. Vizio: Vizio did not provide an answer to this question. 17. Can users erase data that has already been collected by your company and its partners? Amazon: > Yes. Customers have a variety of ways to easily manage data Amazon collects, including deletion options. Apple: > At Apple, we respect users’ ability to know, access, correct, transfer, restrict the processing of, and delete their personal data. Users worldwide can delete data associated with their account at the Apple Data and Privacy page at privacy.apple.com. Google: > Users can review, manage, and permanently delete their activity history, voice recordings, and personalized search data via the Google My Activity portal (myactivity.google.com). Hisense: Hisense did not respond to The Verge’s questions despite five attempts to make contact. They also can request deletion of certain data—including voice information and viewing information—directly through the TV’s settings. > When a user withdraws consent or requests deletion, LG deletes the relevant data in accordance with its data retention and deletion policies. Panasonic: Panasonic did not provide an answer to this question. Roku: > Users can submit a deletion request at privacy.roku.com, and we process it in accordance with applicable law. Samsung: > Yes, customers may request to have their data deleted. Customers may also reset their device advertising ID, which means previous Automatic Content Recognition (ACR) data can no longer be associated with their device. Sony: Sony did not provide an answer to this question. TCL: > Users can ask TCL to delete data it has collected through TCL’s official privacy request channels. Vizio: Vizio did not provide an answer to this question.

articles.title: House Democrat rips colleagues who missed Hegseth vote: ‘Shameful’
articles.summary: Democratic Rep. Sydney Kamlager-Dove (Calif.) on Tuesday evening decried the 11 members of her party who missed a House vote to advance impeachment proceedings against Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth. House Republicans effectively tabled the measure, with the chamber voting 211-204 to refer the resolution to committee. No Democrats voted against advancing the measure in the…
articles.body:
Democratic Rep. Sydney Kamlager-Dove (Calif.) on Tuesday evening decried the 11 members of her party who missed a House vote to advance impeachment proceedings against Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth.

House Republicans effectively tabled the measure, with the chamber voting 211-204 to refer the resolution to committee. No Democrats voted against advancing the measure in the Tuesday vote.

“There’s no reason why we should have lost this vote because of attendance issues,” Kamlager-Dove told MeidasTouch’s Pablo Manríquez. “This is what the people have been talking about … so shame on folks who were not here because these people lost.”

She added that several GOP lawmakers “lost and they still found a way to show up to table this bill.”

The California Democrat emphasized her support for Hegseth’s removal, saying the Defense secretary “should have been impeached a long time ago.” GOP Rep. Thomas Massie (Ky.) introduced eight articles of impeachment against Hegseth on Monday.

“We knew this vote was coming, so people should have gotten their raggedy selves up these steps to vote,” Kamlager-Dove said.

Some of the Democratic lawmakers who missed the Tuesday evening vote — including Reps. Melanie Stansbury (N.M.), Jonathan Jackson (Ill.) and Laura Gillen (N.Y.) — said they were blocked from reaching the Capitol before the vote closed because of traffic.

“Like other Members of Congress, Rep. Stansbury was blocked from entering the Capitol to vote due a traffic incident and a police escort of a bus during the vote,” the New Mexico Democrat said in a statement on social media after the vote.

“When she reached the chamber, the vote had just gaveled out,” the statement continued. “She immediately filed a report of her vote of ‘NO’ to the motion meant to kill the impeachment articles and refer them to the Judiciary Committee, as documented in the Congressional Record. Pete Hegseth must be impeached now.”

Several retiring Democrats were also among the lawmakers who missed the vote, including Reps. Julia Brownley (Calif.), Nancy Pelosi (Calif.) and Frederica Wilson (Fla.).

Additionally, California Rep. Lou Correa (D) said he “vehemently” supported the impeachment resolution but shared a statement disclosing that he would miss votes while he underwent a “medical procedure here in Orange County.”

Democratic Reps. Steven Horsford (Nev.), Marilyn Strickland (Wash.), Haley Stevens (Mich.) and Brittany Pettersen (Colo.) were also absent.

Other Democratic lawmakers also expressed frustration over the missed votes.

“I don’t know if anyone had any real health issues or anything significant to that respect, so I want to leave room for that, but that being said, at the end of the day we’re here to do a job,” New York Rep. Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez (D) told CNN’s Manu Raju on Tuesday evening following the vote.

“And the same way I had to clock in when I worked at a restaurant, we got to clock in and do our work here,” she added.

articles.body:
President Trump will deliver remarks Wednesday at Arlington National Cemetery to mark Veterans Day and honor U.S. service members and military organizations.

Trump will also participate in a wreath-laying ceremony at the Tomb of the Unknown Soldier alongside first lady Melania Trump, Vice President Vance and second lady Usha Vance, among others. Veterans Affairs Secretary Doug Collins will also be in attendance.

The president is expected to recognize several veterans, including those who served in World War II, Vietnam and Afghanistan.

It comes a day after House Republicans blocked a vote to impeach Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth. The measure was tied to his handling of the Iran war and other recent military operations.

The event is scheduled to begin at 11 a.m. EST.

articles.title: ‘I would vote to impeach’ Hegseth, says Marjorie Taylor Greene
articles.summary: “If I were in Congress today, I would vote to impeach,” Greene said.
articles.body:
( NewsNation ) — Former Rep. Marjorie Taylor Greene (R-Ga.) said Tuesday that she would vote to impeach Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth if she were still in the House.

Greene said Congress needs to reassert its authority over war powers.

“If I were in Congress today, I would vote to impeach,” she told NewsNation. “Congress needs to reclaim its authority over war, and Congress is supposed to vote when a war is lasting more than 60 days. And this has not been reigned in for decades, war after war after war.”

The remarks came ahead of a House vote on Rep. Thomas Massie’s (R-Ky.) eight articles of impeachment against the Defense chief. The effort, lacking support and partially tied to almost a dozen missing Democratic lawmakers , was ultimately shelved .

Greene, a loyal supporter-turned-critic of President Trump, left Congress in January. Her resignation followed a public falling-out with the president, as she criticized him for his stance on files related to convicted sex offender Jeffrey Epstein, along with foreign policy and healthcare.

The Georgia Republican also called for accountability for an explosion that killed scores of Iranian students at a school in late February. Satellite images and expert analysis suggest it was likely caused by U.S. airstrikes that also hit an adjacent compound associated with the regime’s Revolutionary Guard.

“I also agree with the articles about the deaths at the children’s school; that’s something that Secretary Hegseth and the entire Department of War have not been transparent on,” Greene continued. “And this is something that shouldn’t happen. I think those are war crimes.”

Greene was once one of the most vocal and visible supporters of Trump’s “ Make America Great Again ” movement, and she embraced some of his unapologetic political style.

Her break with him was a notable fissure in his grip over conservatives, particularly his most ardent base. But her decision to step down in the face of his opposition put her on the same track as many of the more moderate establishment Republicans before her who went crosswise with Trump.

articles.title: House Democrat: ‘Mr. Hegseth’s days are numbered’
articles.summary: Rep. Madeleine Dean (D-Pa.) on Tuesday evening issued a stark warning to Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth after House Republicans shelved an effort to impeach the Pentagon chief. “I think Mr. Hegseth’s days are numbered,” Dean told NewsNation’s Jackie Koppell. “Whether it’s by impeachment or the president removing him or his own resignation, his days are…
articles.body:
Rep. Madeleine Dean (D-Pa.) on Tuesday evening issued a stark warning to Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth after House Republicans shelved an effort to impeach the Pentagon chief.

“I think Mr. Hegseth’s days are numbered,” Dean told NewsNation’s Jackie Koppell. “Whether it’s by impeachment or the president removing him or his own resignation, his days are numbered.”

Rep. Thomas Massie (R-Ky.) introduced eight articles of impeachment against Hegseth on Monday, but the resolution failed to advance due to Republican opposition and Democratic absences .

Earlier this week, Sen. Ted Cruz (R-Texas) also predicted Hegseth would either resign, be fired or be impeached.

The Texas senator noted during a Monday episode of his podcast that he expects Democrats to take up the measure again when they enter the majority next year.

“And I expect, if Schumer has the option of conducting a trial, I would anticipate that he would conduct an extended trial — that he would spend real time, weeks, if not months, using the trial to prosecute, number one, their opposition to the Iran war,” he said on “Verdict with Ted Cruz,” referring to Senate Minority Leader Chuck Schumer (D-N.Y.).

Democratic Rep. Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez (N.Y.) indicated the effort could be considered even sooner in an interview with CNN following the Tuesday evening vote.

“Hopefully, we don’t even have to wait for the new Congress,” she told CNN’s Manu Raju. “I think that should we have the appropriate numbers, Massie could bring it again or anyone else.”

Dean cited her party’s major victories in last week’s midterms , which flipped control of both chambers of Congress in Democrats’ favor, in her interview with NewsNation on Tuesday evening.

“I do think what this election showed was the American people want accountability, accountability around this war, accountability about how to end this war,” she said. “You saw, Mr. Hegseth didn’t even report the number of dead correctly in his latest statements around this war. It’s shameful.”

The Pennsylvania Democrat also told Politico on Tuesday that she was “considering” challenging Sen. John Fetterman (D-Pa.) in 2028, citing discontent with his legislative record.

articles.title: Nvidia CEO ‘should have known better’: Former FBI special agent
articles.summary: Former FBI special agent Tracy Walder on Tuesday said Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang “should have known better” after admitting he had an affair with an alleged Chinese spy, which is raising concerns over national security. “Now, someone like him, who’s the head of this trillion-dollar company, should have had people around him telling him, ‘No,’…
articles.body:
Former FBI special agent Tracy Walder on Tuesday said Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang “should have known better” after admitting he had an affair with an alleged Chinese spy, which is raising concerns over national security .

“Now, someone like him, who’s the head of this trillion-dollar company, should have had people around him telling him, ‘No,’ right? ‘This is risky. This is a problem,'” Walder told NewsNation’s Brian Entin. “But the bottom line is the answer ultimately lies with him. So they can tell him no but the bottom line is he ultimately decides whether or not he wants to be with her.”

Walder added that “the reality is, is yes, he should have known better.”

Jensen Huang recently acknowledged that he was unfaithful to his wife after an affair with Alice Huang, who The New York Times reported was illegally smuggling advanced AI chips to China during her “close relationship” with the Nvidia CEO, according to American spy agencies.

The affair has led to rare bipartisan calls to open probes into whether the relationship placed U.S. national security at risk. Democratic lawmakers, however, are likely to be more focused on what President Trump knew and when.

Trump told reporters on Sunday that he had not spoken with Jensen Huang, a close ally, and called him an “ honorable guy .”

“I think he probably has an excuse … he’s done an amazing job for our country,” he said.

Sen. Chris Coons (D-Del.) previously told The Hill that a congressional investigation into Trump and the Nvidia CEO’s relationship and what the president knew is “central.”

Three House Republicans across several committees have called on Jensen Huang to testify in a closed-door briefing on his company’s security protocols and his “interactions with a publicly reported People’s Republic of China (PRC) intelligence asset: Megaspeed executive Alice Huang.”

Nvidia previously told The Hill that Megaspeed was a regional customer and that the claims against Alice Huang were debunked last year.

On Tuesday, Nvidia’s board hired former acting U.S. Attorney of the Southern District of New York Joon H. Kim to conduct an independent investigation into the CEO and the relationship with Alice Huang.

The board said it has “confidence in Jensen and his leadership team,” and that there was “no reason to believe that either national security or NVIDIA secrets” were compromised.
